header.deal: Restaurant-supply distributor (kitchen equipment, disposables) with 14 branches
header.tag_why: The CFO committed once Wen put a dollar figure on her manual matching hours and unmatched-deposit write-offs, built from her own statements ('that's my number, not yours'); payout reconciliation was the capability, but the deciding comparison was its cost to her.

evidence.excerpt: I thought it was the online ordering portal. That's what the inbound said.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: She'd been there about four months, and her first month-end close took nine days.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: two people in finance matching deposits from the bank against the processor statements against invoices in the ERP. By hand, in spreadsheets.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Paul's team is four people and they aren't building anything. The portal is off the shelf with a plugin.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: The inbound named a portal, but the evaluation really came from a new CFO's nine-day first close and two people matching deposits by hand. The rep's own story contradicts itself: they were 'building a portal' at first, then the portal turns out to be an off-the-shelf plugin, so a checkout or API pitch never had a buyer here. The real problem only surfaced around the third call.
trigger.messaging: For finance-led buyers, open on month-end close and deposit-to-invoice matching (M9), not checkout, even when the inbound mentions an ordering portal.

evidence.excerpt: I can recommend, she decides.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: And she's the one who signed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Paul had forwarded it to her, she read the first page and said it wasn't her problem.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Then nothing happened for three weeks.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: Ines decided, and two facts confirm it: Paul said so and she signed. The first proposal was written for the recommender, and the decider dismissed it after one page, which cost three silent weeks. A rep only learns that kind of loss after the fact.
decider.messaging: Write page one of every proposal for the finance owner's problem in her words (where the money is, month-end), with checkout and APIs as supporting detail.

evidence.excerpt: I honestly don't know what Fiserv showed them, if anything. I never saw a deck.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: we can take a look at your rates.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I didn't ask about my rates.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: She did ask us one new thing afterwards, whether she'd get a named contact.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: It is unknown whether Fiserv made any real competitive pitch. The only thing we know the incumbent said was a rate offer, and the CFO rejected that as off-target, so price was not the battleground. The rep said her questions changed 'not much', but the one new question was about a named contact, after her own bank rep had changed without her knowing who the new one was. The incumbent's relationship had decayed, and that was a real opening.
competitor.messaging: Against bank-channel incumbents, don't lead on rates; pair reconciliation visibility with a named person who owns the account, and frame M5 as a person rather than as tiered response times.

evidence.excerpt: Silence was the whole opening. I ran the standard first-call deck.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: They sell to restaurants in three states.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: The reaction was the payout reconciliation.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: go back.
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: M1 (global, every currency) and M2 (developers) fell flat with a three-state business whose four-person IT team builds nothing. M9 was the only message that made the decider interrupt the demo. She then immediately asked to see it on her own data, which means the generic demo created interest but did not create belief.
message.messaging: Promote M9 to the opener for distributors and invoice-based businesses, and offer the own-data walkthrough in the same breath.

evidence.excerpt: Then she asked if she could see it with their data.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Wen asked for one month of their statements, the controller sent them over
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: that's my number, not yours.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Dead, honestly. I had it at 20 percent.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: By the rep's own estimate, one meeting took the deal from 'Dead' to signed. What moved it was a cost figure built from the customer's statements and her own people costs, not our claims. That is the opposite of M6's 'independent economic impact study', and Ines explicitly valued it because it was not ours. Nobody can recall the exact figure, so the most persuasive asset in the deal isn't reusable as told.
decided.messaging: Recast M6 from 'proven ROI, independent study' to an offer: send one month of statements and we'll show what manual matching costs you.

evidence.excerpt: She wanted to talk to another distributor. Wholesale, invoices, that kind of business.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: this is a company that sells sweaters.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: We never got her a call. She signed anyway, but she brought it up twice.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Wen said yes and showed a slide. We didn't demo it. She let it go.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: We had no distributor or wholesale peer to offer, and the retail substitute made our proof look irrelevant to her. She raised it twice, so 'paperwork' after the ROI meeting understates what was still open. The branch counter readers landing in the same report is an M3 claim backed only by a slide. The transcript doesn't say whether the 14 branches are in the signed scope, so this is a live delivery risk.
gaps.messaging: M8 needs a wholesale or distributor reference with invoice-based reconciliation, and M3 should be backed by a demo of counter and online sales in one payout report, not a slide.

evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I just want to know where my money is.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: She never once said 'payments.' She'd say 'the deposits.'
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Paul would say 'the processor.' Nobody said 'infrastructure.'
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: The buyer described a visibility and close problem, not a payments problem. Our core vocabulary ('financial infrastructure', 'payments') never appeared in her mouth. She thinks in deposits and month-end, and IT thinks of us as 'the processor', a commodity line item.
language.messaging: For finance buyers, swap 'financial infrastructure' for deposit-level language such as 'know where your money is, deposit by deposit, at month-end'.

gaps.question: What did Fiserv or the bank actually propose beyond a rate review, if anything?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ines (or Paul) whether the bank came back with any offer after the rates call, and whether they considered staying.

gaps.question: What changed in their questions after they talked to the bank?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana how much the named-contact answer weighed in the decision, and whether Ines raised service again before signing.

gaps.question: What was the exact dollar figure in the cost analysis?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Wen for the model and the final figure (hours, people cost, write-offs) so it can become a reusable template.

gaps.question: Are the 14 branches' counter card readers part of what was signed, or online only?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana and Wen what scope is in the contract, and whether the counter-to-report flow has been demoed or tested on their data.

gaps.question: Does Ines still want a distributor reference post-signature?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana whether the reference request is still open, and ask customer marketing whether any wholesale or distributor customer could take that call.

close.rep_takeaway: The inbound tells you what someone typed, not who owns the pain. On call one, ask who signs and what finance does at month-end. Once the buyer reacts, get her data on the table fast: 'that's my number, not yours' beat every slide we had. Write the number down so the next rep can use it.
